## Overview

The Tagalog are an Austronesian ethnic group native to the Philippines, especially Metro Manila, Calabarzon, and Marinduque in southern Luzon. They comprise majorities in Bulacan, Bataan, Nueva Ecija, Aurora, Zambales, and Mindoro, and Tagalog-speaking populations also live in Palawan and many parts of Mindanao. Their settlements are generally lowland and commonly oriented toward river deltas, riverbanks, and the wawà, or mouth of a river. Tagalog is a Central Philippine language within the Austronesian family and is closely related to Bikol, Bisayan, Ilocano, Kapampangan, and Pangasinan. Filipino, its standardized and codified form, is the national language of the Philippines. Tagalog folk culture includes lowland maritime histories, barangay social organization, anito beliefs, distinctive regional cuisines, naming customs, poetic forms, and the continued influence of Spanish colonial Christianity.

## Material culture

### Architecture

Tagalog settlements are described as generally lowland communities oriented toward riverbanks, deltas, and the wawà. Pre-Hispanic barangays were maritime settlements, most of them networked almost exclusively by sea traffic. The bayan of the Pasig River delta served as a major political and commercial center, while larger towns included Cebu, Butuan, Jolo, and Cotabato. The sources mention temples in the form of forts or enlarged huts with palisades, and houses where larauan, or religious images, could be kept. They also describe Tagalog sacred places including caves, ancient cemeteries, rivers, lakes, mountains, and trees. Specific house plans, construction materials, roof forms, and architectural ornament are not covered.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 Historical trade records state that Ma-i imported manufactured wares, iron, and jewelry, while Tondo-Maynila retailed Chinese and Japanese manufactured goods throughout the Philippine archipelago. The religious sources name fishing gear, fishhooks, nets, boats, houses, and larauan, or images representing deities, as objects associated with offerings and ritual practice.

### Jewelry & body adornment

 They mention gold among objects that could be offered during anito rites and describe anting-anting as an amulet associated with sacred sites.

## Music & performance

 They describe *pag-aanito*, also called *manganito* or *baylán*, as a ritual held for a sick chief. In the account attributed to the anonymous 1572 *Relación de la conquista de la isla de Luzón*, a chief invited relatives, prepared a feast of fish, meat, and wine, and gathered with priestesses and older men. The participants placed the idol called Batala among them, offered it some of the food, and prayed for the sick man’s health. The ceremony was reported to last seven or eight days. The sources also state that pre-Hispanic Tagalogs honored spirits with rituals and feast days connected with birth, sickness, death, courtship, marriage, planting, and harvesting.

## Dance & theatre

 They mention the epic *Florante at Laura* and the poetic form *tanaga*.

## Festivals & rituals

 They describe religious rites centered on *anito*, a term applied to deities, non-ancestral spirits, and ancestral spirits. Pre-Hispanic Tagalogs honored these beings through rituals and feast days associated with birth, sickness, death, courtship, marriage, planting, harvesting, and death.

A ritual called *pag-aanito*, also known as *manganito* or *baylán*, could be held when a chief was ill. Relatives gathered for a meal of fish, meat, and wine, while priestesses and older men offered food to Batala and prayed for the sick person. The sources say that the ceremony usually lasted seven or eight days. They also describe *dambana* practices, including thanksgiving, wish prayers, and memorializing an event. Sacred sites included Lake Taal and Volcano, Mount Cristobal, Mount Banahaw, Mount Makiling, the Southern Sierra Madre, Laguna de Bay, the Pasig River, Mount Arayat, Marinduque, ancient ruins, and caves.

Tagalog naming customs formed part of early life-cycle practice. Infants were named soon after birth, usually according to circumstances surrounding the birth. A surname was traditionally given upon the birth of the first child, with fathers adding *Amani* and mothers adding *Ynani*. The sources also describe conversion to Roman Catholic Christianity, baptism, and the adoption of Christian first names.

## Foodways

Rice is the primary staple food in Tagalog cuisine, while tubers are typically prepared as vegetables. Palm vinegar, soy sauce, calamansi, chilis, garlic, and onions are commonly combined in dishes. Seafood and pork are prominent, alongside poultry and beef. Panaderias, or neighborhood bakeries, were inherited from Hispanic culture.

Cuisine is organized mainly by town, province, or region rather than by centralized culinary institutions. Bulacan is associated with chicharon, puto, suman, sapin-sapin, ube halaya, kutsinta, cassava cake, and pastillas de leche. Rizal is known for suman and cashew products, while Laguna is associated with buko pie and panutsa. Batangas is associated with kapeng barako, lomi, bulalo, and goto. Batangas also has Taal Lake, whose freshwater fish include maliputo and tawilis, both identified as local delicacies.

*Bistek Tagalog* consists of strips of sirloin beef cooked slowly in soy sauce, calamansi juice, vinegar, and onions. Records identify kare-kare as the Tagalog dish first tasted by the Spanish when they landed in pre-colonial Tondo. Roadside eateries serve local specialties, and Batangas has numerous lomihan, gotohan, and bulalohan.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe the *tanaga* as an indigenous artistic poetic form associated with the Tagalog people. They identify Francisco Baltazar, also called Francisco Balagtas, as the foremost Tagalog writer and name *Florante at Laura* as his notable early nineteenth-century epic. Francisco Baltazar lived from 1788 to 1862.

The controversial *Maragtas* manuscript is described as an origin narrative involving ten datus and their followers, migration from Borneo to Panay, and the figures Rajah Makatunaw, Kalengsusu, Puti, and Dumaksol. The account connects Kalengsusu and Dumaksol with the Taal river area in present-day Batangas and presents their barangay followings as an origin of the Tagalogs. The sources also mention the Laguna copperplate inscription, whose Old Malay text contains place names and information relevant to early Tagalog history.

## Language & religion

Tagalog is a Central Philippine language in the Austronesian family. It is closely related to Bikol, Bisayan, Ilocano, Kapampangan, and Pangasinan, and more distantly related to other Austronesian languages. It commonly uses verb-subject-object order but can also use subject-verb-object order. Tagalog is agglutinative, has a trigger system of morphosyntactic alignment, and is written today with the Latin alphabet. Before Spanish colonization, it was written in an abugida called *Baybayin*. The first known complete book written in Tagalog was *Doctrina Christiana*, printed in 1593.

Tagalog religion consists mainly of Austronesian religious elements supplemented by Hinduism, Mahayana Buddhism, and Islam. Spanish priests referred to it as *tagalismo*. The belief in *anito* is sometimes called Anitism. Bathala is the supreme creator and conserver, while other beings include Mayari, Apolaki, Tala, Hanan, Lakapati, Makiling, and Sitan. The soul has two forms: the living *kakambal* and the posthumous *kaluluwa*. Good ancestral spirits go to Maca, while evil ancestral spirits go to Kasamaan or Kasanaan. Tagalog religious practice also includes *katulunan*, spiritual practitioners who could be male or female, although the sources describe the role as most often female.
